subject: Reasoning
topic: Dot Situation & Grouping of Identical Figures

questions.stem: A dot (•) is placed in a region that lies inside a large circle and inside a triangle, but outside a square. The square, triangle, and circle all partially overlap one another. Which of the following correctly identifies the region occupied by the dot?

options.option_text: Inside the circle and the square, but outside the triangle
Inside the circle and the triangle, but outside the square
Inside the square and the triangle, but outside the circle
Inside all three shapes: the circle, square, and triangle

questions.explanation: B is correct. The problem explicitly states three membership conditions: dot is inside the circle (✓), inside the triangle (✓), and outside the square (✓). The dot therefore occupies the region (circle ∩ triangle) minus the square. Option D fails immediately: the dot is outside the square, so it cannot be inside all three shapes. Option A contradicts the given condition by placing the dot inside the square. Option C contradicts the given condition by placing the dot outside the circle. Step-by-step rule for dot situation: evaluate each shape's membership independently — the correct answer must satisfy every stated condition simultaneously, not just two out of three. Examiners often make one of the wrong options satisfy two of the three conditions to create a tempting near-miss.

questions.stem: Six arrow figures labeled 1 to 6 are described: Arrow 1 points Right; Arrow 2 points Left; Arrow 3 points Upward; Arrow 4 points Left; Arrow 5 points Right; Arrow 6 points Upward. Which of the following gives the correct grouping of identical figures?

options.option_text: Group I: {1,3}, Group II: {2,4}, Group III: {5,6}
Group I: {1,5}, Group II: {2,4}, Group III: {3,6}
Group I: {1,4}, Group II: {2,5}, Group III: {3,6}
Group I: {1,2}, Group II: {3,5}, Group III: {4,6}

questions.explanation: B is correct. Match each arrow's direction one by one: Arrow 1 (Right) = Arrow 5 (Right) → Group {1,5}. Arrow 2 (Left) = Arrow 4 (Left) → Group {2,4}. Arrow 3 (Up) = Arrow 6 (Up) → Group {3,6}. Option A groups {1,3} — a Right arrow paired with an Upward arrow — different directions, not identical. Option C groups {1,4} — Right arrow with Left arrow — these point in opposite directions, a classic mismatch trap. Option D groups figures by sequence (1-2, 3-5, 4-6) rather than by matching attributes, which is the most common beginner mistake. Rule: In grouping of identical figures, never group by serial order — always compare every figure against every other for an exact directional and visual match.

questions.stem: Three shapes — a triangle (T), a circle (C), and a rectangle (R) — are drawn so that every pair overlaps with each other, but no single point lies inside all three shapes simultaneously. How many distinct non-overlapping regions does this arrangement create within the area covered by at least one of the three shapes?

options.option_text: Exactly 5 distinct non-overlapping regions inside the shapes
Exactly 6 distinct non-overlapping regions inside the shapes
Exactly 7 distinct non-overlapping regions inside the shapes
Exactly 8 distinct non-overlapping regions inside the shapes

questions.explanation: B is correct. List every possible distinct non-overlapping region created by pairwise overlaps: (1) Only inside T, (2) Only inside C, (3) Only inside R, (4) Inside T∩C but not R, (5) Inside T∩R but not C, (6) Inside C∩R but not T. The triple-intersection region T∩C∩R = ∅ (explicitly given), so that 7th slot does not exist. Total = 6. Option C (7) is the full three-circle Venn diagram answer — valid only when all three shapes also share a common triple-overlap area. Option A (5) is a miscounting error where students forget one of the three pairwise-overlap bands. Option D (8) has no logical basis for three shapes. Quick formula: a full Venn diagram for 3 shapes gives 2³ − 1 = 7 regions; removing the unavailable triple intersection gives 7 − 1 = 6. This counting skill identifies how many distinct dot positions exist in a given figure.

questions.stem: A circle (C) is drawn entirely inside a triangle (T). A square (S) overlaps with the triangle (T) but does not touch or overlap with the circle (C) at all. A dot is placed randomly inside this figure. For which of the following regional memberships does a valid dot position EXIST in this arrangement?

options.option_text: Inside the circle, inside the triangle, and inside the square
Inside the circle and triangle, but entirely outside the square
Inside the circle and square, but entirely outside the triangle
Inside the square and circle, while being outside the triangle

questions.explanation: B is correct. Apply two rules systematically: Rule 1 — Containment: C lies entirely inside T (C ⊂ T), meaning any point inside C is automatically inside T as well. So 'inside C, inside T, outside S' is valid — and is achievable because C and S do not overlap. Rule 2 — Non-overlap: C ∩ S = ∅ (given), so any point inside C is outside S. Option A fails because it requires inside C ∩ S — impossible since those two shapes do not overlap. Options C and D both require the dot to be inside C while being outside T — impossible because C ⊂ T is an absolute containment; there is no part of C that exists outside T. Step-by-step pattern: First build the containment chain (C ⊂ T forces inside C → inside T). Then use non-overlap (C ∩ S = ∅ forces inside C → outside S). These two rules together eliminate three wrong options without needing to draw the figure.

questions.stem: Six figures (1–6) each show a square containing a diagonal arrow. Figure 1: solid arrow pointing up-right. Figure 2: solid arrow pointing up-right. Figure 3: hollow (outline-only) arrow pointing up-right. Figure 4: solid arrow pointing down-left. Figure 5: hollow arrow pointing up-right. Figure 6: solid arrow pointing down-left. Which of the following is the correct grouping of identical figures?

options.option_text: Group I: {1,2}, Group II: {3,5}, Group III: {4,6}
Group I: {1,3}, Group II: {2,6}, Group III: {4,5}
Group I: {1,4}, Group II: {2,5}, Group III: {3,6}
Group I: {1,6}, Group II: {2,3}, Group III: {4,5}

questions.explanation: A is correct. Two attributes define each figure: (i) fill style — solid vs hollow, and (ii) direction — up-right vs down-left. Match both for every pair: Fig 1 and 2 → both solid, both up-right → identical → {1,2}. Fig 3 and 5 → both hollow, both up-right → identical → {3,5}. Fig 4 and 6 → both solid, both down-left → identical → {4,6}. Option B traps students who group {1,3} based on shared direction (both up-right) while ignoring the fill difference (solid vs hollow) — a genuine attribute mismatch. Option C traps students who group {1,4} based on shared fill (both solid) while ignoring opposite directions — also not identical. Key rule: In SSC grouping of identical figures, EVERY attribute must match simultaneously — direction, fill style, shape, and size. A single attribute difference disqualifies the pair. Examiners frequently insert a subtle style variation (solid vs outline) as the discrimination cue precisely because candidates focus only on direction.

questions.stem: Four shapes are layered as follows: a large pentagon (P) is outermost; a circle (C) lies entirely inside P; a rectangle (R) overlaps with C and also extends partially outside P; a triangle (T) lies entirely within the overlap region of C and R (that is, T ⊆ C ∩ R). A dot is placed inside T. Which of the following correctly identifies ALL shapes the dot is inside, and ALL it is outside of, among {P, C, R, T}?

options.option_text: Dot lies inside all four shapes simultaneously: T, C, R, and P
Dot is inside T, C, R only — outside P, since R extends beyond P
Dot is inside T and C only — outside both R and P entirely
Dot is inside T, C, and P only — outside R, since R is external

questions.explanation: A is correct. Trace the full containment chain step by step: Step 1 — T ⊆ C ∩ R means T is inside both C and R simultaneously, so the dot is inside C and inside R. Step 2 — C ⊆ P (given: C lies entirely inside P). Since the dot is inside C, and C is entirely within P, transitivity gives: dot is inside P as well. Conclusion: dot is inside T, C, R, and P — all four. Option B is the primary trap: students note that R extends outside P and incorrectly reason that T (being inside R) must also lie outside P. The fatal flaw in that logic: T is inside C (from T ⊆ C ∩ R), and C is entirely inside P — so T cannot lie outside P regardless of how far R extends beyond P. This is the transitivity trap: A ⊆ B ⊆ C forces A ⊆ C, even when a fourth shape D overlaps with A but extends outside C. Option D contradicts T ⊆ C ∩ R by claiming T is outside R — directly contradicted by the given containment. Pattern rule: In multi-shape dot situations, always build the full containment chain (T⊆C⊆P) before checking any individual overlap — the chain overrides piecemeal overlap reasoning.

questions.stem: Six figures (1–6) each depict a letter-like shape based on 'F'. Figure 1: standard F (arms open rightward), upper horizontal arm longer than lower. Figure 2: standard F, lower horizontal arm longer than upper. Figure 3: mirror-image F (arms open leftward), upper arm longer. Figure 4: mirror-image F, upper arm longer. Figure 5: standard F, lower horizontal arm longer than upper. Figure 6: standard F, upper horizontal arm longer than lower. Which of the following correctly groups all identical figures?

options.option_text: Group I: {1,6}, Group II: {2,5}, Group III: {3,4}
Group I: {1,3}, Group II: {2,4}, Group III: {5,6}
Group I: {1,4}, Group II: {2,3}, Group III: {5,6}
Group I: {1,2}, Group II: {3,6}, Group III: {4,5}

questions.explanation: A is correct. Three attributes must match: (i) orientation — standard F vs mirror-F; (ii) which arm is longer — upper vs lower. Systematic matching: Fig 1 (standard F, upper longer) = Fig 6 (standard F, upper longer) → {1,6}. Fig 2 (standard F, lower longer) = Fig 5 (standard F, lower longer) → {2,5}. Fig 3 (mirror-F, upper longer) = Fig 4 (mirror-F, upper longer) → {3,4}. Option B is the primary trap: {1,3} pairs a standard-F and a mirror-F with the same arm proportion. Candidates who compare only arm proportions (upper longer vs lower longer) and ignore the orientation flip will pick this. But a standard F and its mirror image cannot be superimposed by any rotation — they require reflection, making them genuinely different figures in SSC grouping questions. Option C similarly pairs {1,4}: standard-F upper-longer with mirror-F upper-longer — same arm proportion, opposite orientation, not identical. Decisive rule: In SSC CGL grouping of identical figures, a figure and its mirror image are always different groups; you must match orientation AND internal proportions as a joint condition, never either attribute alone.
